beginner.summary: For developers, system administrators, SREs and support engineers who use networked systems every day but have never looked at what their hosts actually put on the wire. Works entirely from the Linux host's point of view in a lab of network namespaces and veth pairs: layered models and encapsulation, Ethernet framing and MTU, ARP and the neighbour table, the IPv4 header and fragmentation, CIDR arithmetic, the host routing table, ICMP, IPv6 addressing, Neighbor Discovery and SLAAC, DHCPv4, UDP, the TCP handshake and state machine, tcpdump and Wireshark, source NAT with nftables, sockets in Python and a layer-by-layer fault-finding method, ending with a two-subnet Linux router capstone.
prerequisites: Uses a Linux shell confidently: running commands with sudo, editing files and reading man pages
Can write and run a short Python 3 script
Has a Linux VM or laptop (any current distribution with kernel 5.15 or later) with root access, iproute2, nftables, tcpdump and Wireshark installed
outcomes: Build isolated multi-subnet labs with ip netns, veth pairs and Linux bridges and reason about each hop
Explain and verify Ethernet, ARP, IPv4, IPv6, ICMP, UDP and TCP behaviour from packet captures
Read and change host addresses, routes, neighbour entries and NAT rules with ip, ss and nft
Find the failing layer in a connectivity fault using a repeatable, evidence-based method
